TP5 — Principal Component Analysis (PCA) part 2

More PCA - heart failure dataset

Massimo Andreatta

2026-07-23

How to use this notebook. You do not need any programming experience. Read each short explanation, then press the green play button (▶) at the top-right of each grey code chunk to run it. Look at the output, and answer the Questions in the green boxes (write your answers in plain text under each one). The goal is to understand the data and the method, not to memorise code.

Building on TP4. This notebook assumes you have completed TP4, which introduced the core ideas of PCA using the hepatitis C dataset. Here we go further: we will look at how variable correlations motivate PCA, how binary clinical variables project onto PCA space, and how to think more carefully about what each principal component captures biologically.

RECAP

The problem: too many variables, too few dimensions

In medicine we routinely measure many things about each patient — blood tests, vital signs, imaging findings. When there are six, ten, or fifty measurements per patient, it becomes impossible to see the data: you cannot draw a 50-dimensional scatter plot. Yet a lot of information in those measurements is redundant — for example, two liver enzymes that always rise together carry roughly the same information.

Principal Component Analysis (PCA) exploits this redundancy to compress many variables into a small number of new variables — the principal components — that still capture most of the interesting variation. Think of it as finding the best angle from which to photograph a 3-D sculpture: you lose one dimension, but if you choose the right angle you preserve the important structure.

What PCA can — and cannot — do

PCA is an unsupervised method: it looks only at the measurements, with no knowledge of clinical outcomes. It will find the directions of greatest variation, which may or may not align with what we care about clinically. When the main sources of biological variation do align with disease severity or prognosis, PCA makes that structure visible. When they do not (for instance, if the dominant variation is technical noise), PCA can mislead. Always interpret the components biologically before drawing conclusions.

Key vocabulary

Term Plain-language meaning
Principal component (PC) A new axis through the data; a weighted combination of the original variables
Score A patient’s coordinate on a PC — where they sit along that axis
Loading How much each original variable contributes to a PC (its “weight” on that axis)
Variance explained The % of total spread captured by a PC — larger means more informative
Scree plot A bar chart of variance explained by each PC, used to decide how many to keep
Biplot A combined plot showing both patient scores and variable loadings

THE DATASET: HEART FAILURE CLINICAL RECORDS

Heart failure occurs when the heart cannot pump enough blood to meet the needs of the body. When the heart cannot pump properly, the body fails to get sufficient oxygen and nutrients.

This dataset contains clinical measurements from 299 heart failure patients admitted to a hospital in Faisalabad, Pakistan (Ahmad T et al. 2017, PLOS ONE). Each row is one patient; each column is a clinical measurement or risk factor recorded at admission.

Variable Description Units
age Age of the patient years
anaemia Decrease of red blood cells (0 = no, 1 = yes) binary
creatinine_phosphokinase CPK enzyme level — marker of muscle damage mcg/L
diabetes Whether the patient has diabetes (0/1) binary
ejection_fraction % of blood pumped out per heartbeat %
high_blood_pressure Hypertension (0/1) binary
platelets Platelet count kiloplatelets/mL
serum_creatinine Serum creatinine — marker of kidney function mg/dL
serum_sodium Serum sodium level mEq/L
sex Sex (0 = female, 1 = male) binary
smoking Smoking status (0/1) binary
time Follow-up period until death or end of study days
DEATH_EVENT Died during follow-up (0 = no, 1 = yes) binary

Load the data

hf <- read.csv("../data/CVD/heart_failure_clinical_records_dataset.csv")

1 — Meet the data

Structure and variable types

The dimensionality of the dataset tells us how many patients and how many variables were measured

dim(hf)
## [1] 299  13

The str command gives an overview of the dataset’s structure

str(hf)

Some variables are continuous measurements (age, ejection fraction, creatinine…); others are binary flags (diabetes, smoking, death event). PCA works on continuous numbers, so we separate them up front.

# Continuous clinical measurements
cont_vars <- c("age", "creatinine_phosphokinase", "ejection_fraction",
               "platelets", "serum_creatinine", "serum_sodium")

# Binary variables — used later to *interpret* PCA, not as PCA input
bin_vars <- c("anaemia", "diabetes", "high_blood_pressure",
              "sex", "smoking", "DEATH_EVENT")

We also exclude time (follow-up length in days). Its value is partly determined by when a patient died — feeding it into PCA and then colouring by death outcome would be circular reasoning.

summary(hf[, cont_vars])

Question 1.1. How many patients are in the dataset, and how many continuous variables will we use for PCA? What does ejection_fraction measure, and why might a value below 40 % be clinically worrying?

Question 1.2. From the summary() output, which variable has the largest numerical range? Does a large range mean that variable is more biologically important, or is it simply a consequence of the units in which it is measured?

Spotting skewed distributions and log-transforming

Right-skewed variables (a long right tail of very high values) can distort PCA — a handful of extreme patients would drag the axes. Let us inspect the two enzyme measurements.

par(mfrow = c(1, 4))
hist(hf$creatinine_phosphokinase, breaks = 40, col = "steelblue",
     main = "CPK (original)", xlab = "mcg/L")
hist(log(hf$creatinine_phosphokinase), breaks = 40, col = "darkorange",
     main = "log(CPK)", xlab = "log mcg/L")
hist(hf$serum_creatinine, breaks = 40, col = "steelblue",
     main = "Serum creatinine (original)", xlab = "mg/dL")
hist(log(hf$serum_creatinine), breaks = 40, col = "darkorange",
     main = "log(Serum creatinine)", xlab = "log mg/dL")

par(mfrow = c(1, 1))

The log transformation makes both distributions far more symmetric. We work with the log-transformed versions from here on.

hf$log_cpk       <- log(hf$creatinine_phosphokinase)
hf$log_creatinine <- log(hf$serum_creatinine)

cont_clean <- c("age", "log_cpk", "ejection_fraction",
                "platelets", "log_creatinine", "serum_sodium")

Question 1.3. Why is it a good idea to log-transform heavily right-skewed variables before PCA? Hint: think about what happens to the Euclidean distance between patients when one variable spans a range of e.g. 1–1000 while another spans 100–150.

2 — Why standardise before PCA?

PCA finds the directions of maximum variance. If one variable has much larger numbers than another (e.g. platelet count in thousands vs. serum sodium in mEq/L), it will dominate the result simply because of its scale — not because it is more informative.

round(apply(hf[, cont_clean], 2, sd, na.rm = TRUE), 3)
##               age           log_cpk ejection_fraction         platelets 
##            11.895             1.134            11.835         97804.237 
##    log_creatinine      serum_sodium 
##             0.453             4.412
X <- scale(hf[, cont_clean])    # standardise to mean 0, sd 1

round(apply(X, 2, mean), 3)     # confirm: all ≈ 0
##               age           log_cpk ejection_fraction         platelets 
##                 0                 0                 0                 0 
##    log_creatinine      serum_sodium 
##                 0                 0
round(apply(X, 2, sd),   3)     # confirm: all = 1
##               age           log_cpk ejection_fraction         platelets 
##                 1                 1                 1                 1 
##    log_creatinine      serum_sodium 
##                 1                 1

After standardisation every variable contributes on equal footing: we compare patterns of variation, not raw magnitudes.

Question 2.1. Before scaling, which variable has the largest standard deviation? If we ran PCA on the raw numbers, which variable would likely dominate PC1 — and would that reflect biology or something else?

Question 2.2. After standardisation, a patient has a value of +2 for ejection_fraction. What does that mean in plain English — how does this patient compare to the rest of the cohort?

3 — Running PCA

Computing the principal components

prcomp() rotates the data so that the first axis (PC1) captures as much variance as possible, the second (PC2) captures as much of the remaining variance as possible, and so on. The total number of PCs equals the number of input variables (here, six).

pca <- prcomp(X, scale. = FALSE)   # already scaled above
summary(pca)
## Importance of components:
##                           PC1    PC2    PC3    PC4    PC5    PC6
## Standard deviation     1.2069 1.0869 0.9895 0.9578 0.8885 0.8222
## Proportion of Variance 0.2428 0.1969 0.1632 0.1529 0.1316 0.1127
## Cumulative Proportion  0.2428 0.4397 0.6029 0.7558 0.8873 1.0000

The row Proportion of Variance tells us how much of the total information each PC captures.

4 — Patients in PCA space

The PCA plot

Each patient becomes a single point in PCA space. Points close together are clinically similar across all six measurements; points far apart differ substantially. Crucially, the PCA was computed without any knowledge of who died — we now colour the points by outcome to see whether the structure aligns with survival.

scores <- as.data.frame(pca$x)
scores$death <- factor(hf$DEATH_EVENT, levels = c(0, 1),
                       labels = c("Survived", "Died"))
col_death <- ifelse(scores$death == "Died", "tomato", "steelblue")

plot(scores$PC1, scores$PC2,
     col = col_death, pch = 19, cex = 0.8,
     xlab = "PC1", ylab = "PC2",
     main = "PCA plot — coloured by outcome")
legend("topright", legend = c("Survived", "Died"),
       col = c("steelblue", "tomato"), pch = 19, cex = 0.9)

Question 4.1. Do patients who died tend to cluster in a specific region of the PC1–PC2 plane? Is the separation between survivors and non-survivors perfect, or is there considerable overlap? What does substantial overlap tell us about the complexity of predicting heart failure outcomes from these measurements alone?

Mapping individual clinical variables onto the PCA

We can colour the same point cloud by any continuous measurement to reveal which variable “explains” the position of patients along each PC axis.

# Helper: map numeric values to a blue-white-red gradient
map_color <- function(x, n = 100) {
  pal <- colorRampPalette(c("blue", "white", "red"))(n)
  idx <- cut(x, breaks = n, labels = FALSE, include.lowest = TRUE)
  pal[idx]
}
par(mfrow = c(1, 3))

plot(scores$PC1, scores$PC2, pch = 19, cex = 0.7,
     col = map_color(hf$ejection_fraction),
     main = "Ejection fraction (%)", xlab = "PC1", ylab = "PC2")

plot(scores$PC1, scores$PC2, pch = 19, cex = 0.7,
     col = map_color(hf$log_creatinine),
     main = "log(Serum creatinine)", xlab = "PC1", ylab = "PC2")

plot(scores$PC1, scores$PC2, pch = 19, cex = 0.7,
     col = map_color(hf$age),
     main = "Age (years)", xlab = "PC1", ylab = "PC2")

par(mfrow = c(1, 1))

In all plots: blue = low values, red = high values.

Question 4.2. Are these variables higher/lower in the same regions of the plot? what does that say about their correlation?

Plotting binary variables in PCA space

The dataset also contains binary clinical flags — anaemia, diabetes, high blood pressure, smoking, and sex. PCA was computed from the six continuous measurements, but we can still ask: do patients with a given condition tend to cluster in a particular region of PCA space?

bin_labels <- c("anaemia", "diabetes", "high_blood_pressure", "sex", "smoking")
bin_titles <- c("Anaemia", "Diabetes", "High blood pressure",
                "Sex (1 = male)", "Smoking")

bin_col <- c("0" = "steelblue", "1" = "tomato")

par(mfrow = c(2, 3))
for (i in seq_along(bin_labels)) {
  grp <- as.character(hf[[ bin_labels[i] ]])
  plot(scores$PC1, scores$PC2,
       col = bin_col[grp], pch = 19, cex = 0.7,
       main = bin_titles[i],
       xlab = "PC1", ylab = "PC2")
  legend("topright", legend = c("Absent / Female", "Present / Male"),
         col = bin_col, pch = 19, cex = 0.75)
}
par(mfrow = c(1, 1))

Question 4.3. For which binary variables (if any) do you see a clear spatial separation in PCA space — i.e., one group clustering on a particular side of PC1 or PC2? What does this tell us about whether those conditions are associated with the main axes of clinical variation in this cohort?

5 — What drives each PC?

The loadings (stored in pca$rotation) tell us how much each original variable contributes to each PC. A large positive loading means patients with high values of that variable sit at the positive end of the PC; a large negative loading places them at the negative end.

round(pca$rotation[, 1:4], 3)
##                      PC1    PC2    PC3    PC4
## age               -0.385 -0.523  0.020 -0.475
## log_cpk            0.162  0.514  0.164 -0.812
## ejection_fraction  0.307 -0.606  0.024 -0.184
## platelets          0.241 -0.091  0.937  0.147
## log_creatinine    -0.616 -0.114  0.236 -0.132
## serum_sodium       0.543 -0.271 -0.196 -0.206
par(mfrow = c(1, 2), mar = c(4, 9, 3, 2))

barplot(sort(pca$rotation[, 1]),
        horiz = TRUE, las = 1, col = "steelblue", border = NA,
        main = "PC1 loadings", xlab = "Loading value")
abline(v = 0, col = "grey40")

barplot(sort(pca$rotation[, 2]),
        horiz = TRUE, las = 1, col = "darkorange", border = NA,
        main = "PC2 loadings", xlab = "Loading value")
abline(v = 0, col = "grey40")

par(mfrow = c(1, 1))

The sign of a loading and the sign of a PC score

A subtlety worth understanding: the direction of a PC axis (which end is “positive” and which is “negative”) is mathematically arbitrary. PCA can flip an axis and the result is equally valid — the relative positions of patients do not change. This means you should always interpret the sign of a loading in the context of the other loadings on the same PC: what matters is whether two variables load in the same or opposite direction, not whether the loading is positive or negative in isolation.

Question 5.1. Looking at the PC1 loading barplot, which variables have the strongest positive and negative loadings? Based on these, propose a biological interpretation for PC1: is it primarily an axis of kidney function, cardiac function, or a contrast between the two?

Question 5.2. Do ejection_fraction and log_creatinine have loadings of the same sign or opposite signs on PC1? A failing heart pumps less blood to the kidneys, causing creatinine to rise — so patients with low ejection fraction often have high serum creatinine. Does the loading barplot reflect this clinical anti-correlation?

Question 5.3. Which variables load most strongly on PC2? What might PC2 represent? (Hint: look at which variables are not well captured by PC1 and therefore have most of their signal in PC2.)

Question 5.4. How would you change the code to also look at PC3 or PC4? How many PCs does it make sense to analyze? How many total PCs are there?
